Interesting experiment between Opus 5.5 and Argon. I'm glad to see I'm not the only one having usage issues with Argon.

I was an early supporter of Gemini because I loved the versatility of a lot of its products. I wanted to test out Argon today after burning through usage at about 15% per pop just talking to it yesterday. I use AI tools to help me with my creative writing, especially for keeping track of past character interactions and timeline continuity. I wrote an outline of the next chapter and put it into both Argon and Opus with the usual context files like my style guide, past writings, character map, etc. The first prompt gave them my outline and told them to rewrite it, improve it and flesh out some subsection and scene ideas. Both AIs gave me a fleshed out version of my outline with the exact same structure I gave them. The second prompt was to completely disregard the outline and create something new. The third prompt I showed them the output of the other AI and asked them to evaluate it and rewrite the other's outline in a better way. The fourth prompt I showed each the other AI's third result and told them to rewrite it using the same structure as the other. The fifth prompt I showed them the results of the 4th and told them to take the best parts of all 4 outlines and create the final version. The totally odd thing is what came out of the 5th prompt was almost identical between Argon High and Opus 5.5 High. I had to stop at this point because Argon High was out of usage, but Opus 5.5 High was only at 41% usage. Absolutely ridiculous and the outcome was a little creepy and bizarre.

I made a Minecraft mod to prompt agents who build in the world using the existing terrain as specs

This mod is basically WorldEdit but with AI : First off you select your region (by picking two corners or just by looking where you want your structure to be), then you prompt in a chat command. That prompt is sent to the agent along with the selected region, and the agent work in the background then deliver its result and you get a reconstitution of what it did.

You can even use books in lecterns to give additional spatial context.

Opus 5.5 is incredibly good at following precise instructions while also bringing its own creativity, so I think it can be more than just something to toy with and may be an actual reliable tool for builders who want to complete side-stuff.

The way it works is that the mod is calling a separate program running on the system (called the "core") which handles connecting to your Claude or Codex CLI, you even have a nice UI to configure everything from it (what AI provider, what model, effort etc).

The mod is purely server-side, so you can even toy with it in multiplayer and your friends don't need to install anything as long as the host has it.

Vibe-coded with GPT-6 Astra at the beginning, then I pivoted to Claude Opus 5.5 which did much better, I still took some decisions for the overall architecture and API tho. I also care about having something clean, shareable and that doesn't feel janky. The design and ideas are from me.

Despite having to install two things to install to make it work (the Core program and the mod itself) I hope it's easy enough to pick up.

Fully open-source and forkable: https://github.com/Ni-Cobra/worldprompt

REA made me think about the other side: what my own Claude Code agents can't change

Been watching the REA hype lately (point an agent at an app, it works out how a feature works, down to the binary). Neat tool, not here to argue about it.

It made me think about the opposite direction though. I run a one-person trading business on Claude Code: a "CEO" agent plus five role agents (tech, risk, finance, marketing, strategy) that check live data against the backtest daily, write reports and prepare decisions.

What they never get to do is change anything that moves money. Trading code and its config sit in a zone no agent can edit without my approval, however urgent. Headless agents run on an allowlist, everything else gets auto-denied.

It got tested in September: a strategy hit a loss limit I'd fixed before the first trade, and the system closed the position and halted by itself. Restarting needs me typing the approval, not an agent relaying "owner said ok".

tbh agents getting smarter doesn't change any of that. How do you draw the line, hard deny list or mostly prompting?

My AI explains how it's raising its human

Hi all, This week I tried something new (at least for me): I've been using Claude Code daily for a few months, not only for code but as a working partner across all my projects. Over time I built a fairly large setup around it: CLAUDE.md files split by topic, hooks, skills and subagents. At some point I thought it would be fun to let Claude tell the story from its side. That became "My Human is so Cute", a series narrated by Claude about raising a human who's moody, changes his mind and starts new projects before finishing the old ones .. that's me. Each episode explains one real mechanism: - Memory across sessions. Claude forgets everything every morning. We fixed that with handoff files that the next session reads first, and a SessionStart hook that offers to resume them. - Rules that actually get applied. A rule sitting in a file isn't enough. Some things only work as hooks. For example, a Stop hook commits and pushes at every turn in cloud sessions, because the container is ephemeral. - Subagents with narrow jobs. One produces, another judges against observable criteria, and the judge has a veto. I stopped reviewing first drafts myself. - Guardrails. Anything that goes out (sending, publishing, uploading) needs my explicit OK with the full text in front of me, never a summary. Episode 1, about memory: https://youtu.be/dpA2ijeTZFI The harness files will be in a public GitHub repo. First parts link on yt. Under the jokes there's a real question: what does it mean to work every day with something that may or may not have an inner life? I don't have an answer, and the series doesn't pretend to. Happy to answer questions about the setup. That's honestly the part I'd most like feedback on.

I made a Claude Code mod that shows your 5-hour and weekly limits above the prompt and warns you before you hit them

I kept getting blocked mid-week without warning, so I built two small Claude Code mods. They hook into Claude Code's plugin API, so there's no wrapper and no extra process. limits: an always-on band above the prompt 5-hour and weekly usage: a bar, the percent used and a countdown to the reset The percent turns red when your current pace would use up the limit before it resets. You find out on Tuesday, not when you're blocked on Thursday. Context window fill, plus toasts at 75/90/100%. idle-compact: cheaper returns to big chats The prompt cache expires after an hour, so coming back to a 300k-token chat reloads all of it at full price After 40 min idle, it runs /compact while the cache is still warm, so the chat you return to is small It never compacts a chat you reopened cold, since that would cost full price How it works (if you want to build your own): limits renders an AbovePrompt band from the rate-limit readings Claude Code already receives. It shares one reading across all open sessions through the plugin store, so 10 open chats still make only one 1-token Haiku request every 2 min to stay fresh. Install (in terminal claude): /plugin install limits --marketplace Ryan-LT/claude-mods /plugin install idle-compact --marketplace Ryan-LT/claude-mods Repo (MIT): https://github.com/Ryan-LT/claude-mods Feedback and ideas welcome!

Opus 5.5 is INSANE at decompilation / ports

Just decompiled and natively ported StarFox, StarFox 2 and Sonic CD to Windows, Mac and Linux, using Opus 5.5 without REA or similar skills. Claude analyzed the games' roms, built high level hardware runtimes, and added quality of life improvements (resolution, framerate, audio, full controller support, etc.), Even going as far as editing the game's extracted source code to implement features (SuperFX overclocking, True16:9 in Sonic CD). Projects are here: https://github.com/carlosrmz009/littleplanet https://github.com/carlosrmz009/arwing https://github.com/carlosrmz009/arwing2 Prompt was simply: Create a full decompilation of *GAME*, so it can run natively in my PC. EDIT: Fair correction on the terminology: I used "decompilation" too loosely. My actual goal was to see if I could get these games running as native desktop builds and add modern features. At least in Sonic CD's case, the output seems more accurately described as a game-specific emulator plus generated disassembly/static recompilation, rather than a clean reconstruction of the original source code.

In this big 2026, Claude saved me over $10k

There are millions of ways to use Claude. One of my favourite one is to use it to save potentially hundreds of dollars if not thousands. Here are two of the ways I used Claude this year to save over $10k in 2026.

1. There was a concert I wanted to attend in another city. When I looked at prices of hotels, almost all the good hotels hiked their price like 300%. Well not hotels probably, but the booking sites I was checking. So I went to Claude and asked it what would be the best connector to use for it for finding the cheapest best hotels in that case. It suggested "LetsFG" from it's directory. Used it and the offers it gave me were still somewhat expensive, but relatively cheaper than what the booking sites was showing me. And I'm speaking about a massive $800 saving. All that I used was a simple prompt asking what I actually needed. This approach is really good if you're really sensitive with stuffs that people generally complain about like construction/hallway noise, horrible breakfast, no bathtub etc. I'm generally not that sensitive but because Claude can read hundreds of reviews at once using the MCP, I got myself some pretty premium hotels where the reviews were generally more towards the good side.

2. I bought a car this year (this is my second car) for my family. Well it's a minivan for giving space to 7 people. But there was a massive problem that I had NO idea about anything of cars. My first car was a gift from my dad. I again asked Claude if it can help me, so it suggested a connector from it's directory called "CarGurus". After connecting I just told it in basic plain language what I wanted. This was my prompt: "I want a car (probably SUV or a minivan) for a family of 7 people (5 kids) to fit in. I am in USA, and don't get out of NY that easily. It's mostly to move inside the city. I don't want to spend any money on another car in the next 10 years, so the model has to be somewhat advanced for at least surviving around a decade. The rest of the preferences can change depending on price and quality. Find me some deals using the connector of car" And it found me multiple options it gave me which almost all were cool. But I ended up going with the most expensive one it found me which was a 2025 Hybrid Toyota Sienna. coz that one seemed to be the best among the ones it recommended. I had been an offer somewhere else thay was a little better the Sienna but the price was like $10k more which was completely unnecessary. If I didn't know about the Sienna, I would've bought that one and potentially wasted $10k for a model which was way above that I need.

Quick heads up though: the car dealership MCP only works in USA. Sure you can use it from wherever but it only finds deals in the US. And the option I bought was a used car but with only a few thousand mileage. I'm not sure about what it can do on new cars, but you can test it. However the first MCP for hotel is a worldwide one that you can use for everywhere. You can find both of these connectors in the official directory of Claude
